new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the first syllable of the word, stated as holding for every Karnic language (Wanggamala is Karnic, Palku subgroup). The only language-specific evidence is indirect: Blake 1979:191 gives fixed initial stress with a weak third-syllable secondary for the sister/eastern language Pitta-Pitta and calls the western language (= wang1289) 'structurally isomorphic' with it.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned by Bowern. For Pitta-Pitta, Blake 1979:191: weak secondary on the third syllable of four-syllable words, on the fourth when a new morpheme begins there (takuku-lnu); StressTyp2 (Blake & Breen 1971:32) gives secondary on the first syllable of each non-initial polysyllabic morpheme. Nothing recorded for Wanggamala itself.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Wanggamala. Blake 1979:191 notes for Pitta-Pitta that unstressed syllables are not as weak as in English, that function words cliticise to the preceding word, and that in Nora Jacks's rapid speech only the first syllable of a phrase carries much stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Family-level parenthetical in a comparative/classification paper, not a description of Wanggamala; the language-specific description (Blake & Breen 1971, 14 pp. on the western language) could not be opened. Blake 1979's statement is for words in isolation in Pitta-Pitta (pitt1247). Treat the fixed: initial syllable reading as a low-confidence inference until Blake & Breen 1971 is read.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog wang1289 'Wanggamala' (ISO wnm) is the 'western language' of the Pitta-Pitta (Palku) group as defined by Blake 1979:184-185 and Breen 1971:26-27: northern dialect Wangka-Yutjuru (Ida Toby's material; ISO wky has no Glottolog code, Glottolog's PHOIBLE/Lexibank links for wang1289 are labelled 'Wangkayutyuru') and southern dialect Wangka-Manha = Lhanima/Tharlimanha = Wangkamadla (Nora Jacks's material; ISO lnw, no Glottolog code). Its sister is Pitta Pitta pitt1247 (eastern language). The Blake 1979 stress statement (p.191) is explicitly about Pitta-Pitta, and the Bowern 2001 statement is about Karnic as a whole; no opened source describes stress in wang1289 itself.

sources.note: §2.3 Stress, printed p.191: 'Each word pronounced in isolation is marked by a stress on the initial syllable.. In words of more than two syllables, there is a tendency for a secondary stress to appear. It normally appears on the third syllable of words of four syllables.. The secondary stress is quite weak.' sources.note: For Pitta Pitta (pit): 'Place primary stress on the first syllable of every word, and secondary stress on the first syllable of every polysyllabic morpheme that is not the first.. Secondary stress falls on alternates, but not on the last (Blake & Green 1971:32)'. Wanggamala (wnm) appears only in the ISO table; no StressTyp2 entry.

sources.citation: Breen, J.G. 1971. Aboriginal Languages of Western Queensland (Preliminary Version). Linguistic Communications 5:1-88. Melbourne: Monash University. ERIC ED071503
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Survey and lexicostatistic classification. §7 Lanima and §8 Wangka-jutjuru (pp.8-9) describe the corpora (Blake's from Nora Jacks; Breen's from Ida Toby) and the names Wonkamala/Wangkamadla/Wangkamana; §321.3 Palku sub-group (pp.26-27): 'Lanima and Wangka-jutjuru are two dialects of the western language while the remaining dialects form the eastern language'. Nothing on stress or accent anywhere in the 88 pp. (a full-text search for stress/accent found nothing).
